speechtext:
Hon, Marcel Lambert (Edmonton West): Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 17 (2) I gave you notice of my request to raise a question of privilege at the opening of today's proceedings arising out of a statement attributed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) at a meeting last night of the Kingston Junior Chamber of Commerce. The minister is reported to have said:
-and I've been asked by people "when are you going to legislate the white paper on taxation" and the simple answer to that is never.

subtopic: MR. LAMBERT (EDMONTON WEST)-STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON WHITE PAPER ON TAX REFORM AS BASIS FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. LAMBERT (EDMONTON WEST)-STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON WHITE PAPER ON TAX REFORM AS BASIS FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Apparently there was loud cheering and clapping at that meeting. My question of privilege is that the minister has made a statement of policy of the greatest importance outside the House, which is not subject to direct comment, on a matter on which he has rejected giving forthright answers in the House and, because of the equivocal nature of the statement, has created further confusion and doubt in the House and in the country on the subject of proposed tax reform.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave):
That a transcript of all of the remarks of the Minister of Finance to the Kingston Junior Chamber of Commerce on Tuesday, March 9, 1971, be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and that the Minister of Finance be invited to appear before the said committee to explain his remarks concerning the implementation or rejection of the white paper on tax changes, and to indicate clearly both
the timing and the method to be used for any tax changes so as to remove the doubt and confusion now existing in Canada about the government's tax policy, which contribute in large measure to the present economic recession in the country.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. LAMBERT (EDMONTON WEST)-STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON WHITE PAPER ON TAX REFORM AS BASIS FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has given notice to the Chair of his intention to rise on a question of privilege in the sense that he has just indicated.
The hon. member knows that the Chair must determine whether there is a prima facie case of privilege. After having considered the situation as carefully as possible, I must conclude that the circumstances are not such that the Chair could ask the House to consider the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton West.

Hon. members know that on many occasions in the past it has been suggested that it was tantamount to a breach of the privileges of the House when a ministerial statement of policy is made outside the House. I suggest to hon. members that this is a practice which has been adopted over a long period of years. Although hon. members may feel that this gives rise to a grievance, and thus some hon. members might be dissatisfied with such procedure and they may want to suggest that such statements should more properly be made in the House rather than outside. With respect, I suggest to the hon. member for Edmonton West that it cannot be judged that there is a prima facie case of privilege. In the circumstances I cannot put to the House the motion proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (C), 1970-71 REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEES-RULING ON POINT OF ORDER
speechtext:
Perhaps at this point I might refer to the motion offered by the President of the Privy Council on Monday and indicate the conclusion I have reached after giving the matter much thought.
On Monday last, when the President of the Privy Council offered a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 59 to send supplementary estimates to certain standing committees, the hon. member for Winnipeg

March 10, 1971
Supplementary Estimates
North Centre raised a point of order regarding the propriety or, if one wishes, the legality of considering supplementary estimates which are in effect amendments to existing statutes. The hon. member for Edmonton West argued along the same lines. In support of the motion, the President of the Treasury Board claimed that his proposal was amply supported by precedents. He referred to certain guidelines which he suggested should be looked at by the government when proposing such items and that the proposals were entirely within those guidelines.
The minister is right, of course, when he suggests that the introduction and passage of statutory items in supplementary estimates is not an innovation in this House. This is a practice which goes back many years. At the same time, it has never been accepted readily by the House. Our debates record many instances when members have taken exception to the practice. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre himself is not a neophyte in this regard. For example, on March 31, 1952-if he does not mind my going back so far-as reported at page 969 of Hansard of that day he voiced strong objection to an item in the estimates which, he contended, would circumvent section 3 of the Atomic Energy Control Act. Another example of such objection is a statement by the then hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, who stated in part as follows:
You have statutes; you may repeal them; you may amend them; but you cannot do it by supply bills.
Another random selection was picked from page 3,368 of Hansard for March 27, 1961, where the then hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River went on record to oppose this practice and called as his witness the then absent hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Again, on April 1, 1964, as reported at page 1,680 of Hansard, a similar discussion arose.
There are countless other instances which indicate that statutory dollar items have been used in the past but that this practice has not gone unchallenged.
In the situation now before us, the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre and Edmonton West have distinguished so-called statutory items from those which merely propose a transfer of funds. The members take exception to both types of one-dollar items, but the thrust of their objection is against specific items which they suggest are clearly legislative in intent.
In support of their argument the hon. members suggest that the procedural situation has been radically changed by the adoption of the new rules in December of 1968. They urge that in view of the new supply procedures introduced by these rules, statutory dollar items should not be included in supplementary estimates. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre contends that past practice should not be used as a guide in relation to the present machinery for the consideration of estimates. He suggests that when the House eliminated the committee of supply a new situation was created because it was in committee of supply that formal objection had been taken in the past to these one-dollar statutory items.
Those members suggest that there is now no real opportunity for the consideration of such items by the House itself. That, of course, is not entirely correct since the new Standing Orders do provide for such an opportunity, albeit restricted, under the terms of Standing Order 58. Clearly the Standing Orders do provide the machinery for the consideration by the House itself of specific items in the estimates to which the opposition might take exception. However, this opportunity is undoubtedly limited and depends very much on the number of allotted supply days which might still be available by virtue of Standing Order 58. In other words, under the old rules there was unlimited time to consider supplementary estimates, including items intended to amend statutes. Under the new rules there may be only a limited time to consider supplementary estimates.
Is the difference between the two situations so substantial that the past practice of allowing statutory dollar items in the supplementary estimates should now be disallowed? Should the very limited time allotted by Standing Order 58 be restricted to the consideration of what is strictly supply? There is much to be said to support an affirmative answer to these questions.
The argument proposed by the hon. members for Edmonton West and Winnipeg North Centre is cogent. They contend that any rulings that may have been made in the past about dollar items prior to the changes of the rules do not now apply. They suggest that the rules changes were effected to remove the consideration of detailed estimates from the floor of the House but that no decision was ever made that a motion which is tantamount to a legislative enactment should be removed from the floor of the House. They urge that the items which have a legislative effect should not be allowed to be proceeded with by way of items in the supplementary estimates but should be introduced in the usual way, as is done for all other legislation, by way of a bill.
Let us, if you will, examine the items singled out by the hon. members. The first one is vote 35c. It proposes to amend the Pension Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. The vote proposes to repeal schedules A and B of the Pension Act and substitute therefor new schedules A and B as found in vote 35c. At the same time, it seeks to amend section 38(2) and section 38(4) of the Pension Act. Second, vote 35c proposes to repeal the existing schedules in the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act and substitute a schedule set out under the vote, in effect amending two sections of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act.
Schedules A and B of the Pension Act were previously amended by statute, other than an Appropriation Act, in the years 1953-54, 1957-58, 1960-61. Schedule B was amended in 1966-67. None of these amendments was enacted by way of an appropriation measure. Item 10c, affecting the War Veterans Allowance Act, purports to repeal Schedule A of that act and substitute a new Schedule A in this vote. It refers to Schedule A of the War Veterans Allowance Act which was amended in 1957-58, 1960-61 and in 1965 by statutes other than an

subtopic: OPERATION OF FOREIGN SHIPS WITHIN 12-MILE LIMIT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask leave of the House to make a motion under Standing Order 43. I do so for the following reasons. I ask the unanimous consent of the House for my motion to be considered because of the repeated violations of Canadian territorial waters by foreign ships operating off Newfoundland and especially because of the difficulty in enforcing the 12-mile limit which has recently been proclaimed by the government of Canada. I feel that these foreign vessels, operating at will, are flouting Canadian regulations. Among other things, the situation requires, in my view, a sustained military presence in Newfoundland not only to protect Canadian sovereignty in this regard but to protect the rights of Canadian fishermen. I would therefore ask unanimous consent to move, seconded by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall):
That the House refer the question of naval and air surveillance of foreign fishing vessels operating in zones adjacent to the Canadian coast to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
That the committee explore the question of repeated intrusions into Canadian territorial waters by foreign trawlers and draggers and that the committee further explore possible methods of detecting and preventing such intrusions by the use of air and naval components of the Canadian Armed Forces.
That the committee give consideration to the possible stationing of operational maritime command aircraft in Newfoundland.
Mr. Speaker, I hope this motion will receive the unanimous consent of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I can hardly think of a greater delight than listening to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), I can hardly think of a worse fate for a young member like myself than standing up and following him. I am afraid that after his flight of oratory the House will be brought back to earth with rather a dull thud.
I wish to take a moment to set my remarks in context. I think I can best do that by quoting from an article by Professor J. R. Mallory, printed in the Ottawa Law Review, volume 4, No. 1, summer 1970. Professor Mallory dealt with the question of statutory instruments in Canada and said:
Parliament cannot, and should not, attempt to consider in detail all of the great variety of regulations which are necessary in a modern, urban, and highly technological society. It has more important things to do. It must keep a constant and wary eye on the major policy questions which affect the public interest. In spite of the very large flow of legislation which is now necessary, parliamentary time must not be so taken up by the legislative process that opportunity is lacking for the other very necessary parliamentary function under responsible government, which is to keep under constant review the policy and actions of ministers of the Crown.
Professor Mallory went on to say:
Accordingly, the detailed regulations to make the law effective must be made by officials in the name of the government or some statutory public authority. These regulations are no doubt carefully considered. One can be sure that official committees will consider them carefully before they are promulgated. But, unlike acts of Parliament, they will not be publicly debated before they become part of the law. And after they become part of the law there is little chance for them to be reconsidered. In most cases, public debate would not help and is not necessary. What can Parliament say that is essential or constructive on the safe load of a commercial aircraft or the safety precautions necessary in the use of a chemical pesticide, which the experts cannot say with greater authority? Not much. But the problem is as follows. Does the executive agency which makes the regulations stay within the authority provided by the statute? Does it lay down a regulation which unduly restricts the proper liberty of the subject? Does it interfere with the remedies of the subject? Does it interfere with the remedies normally provided by the courts? Who can say? In my view it is the business of Parliament to act as a watchdog for the public interest. I have great confidence in the professional integrity of the public service but I feel that no man should exercise power in the absence of public scrutiny.
Professor Mallory is arguing in favour of parliamentary supervision over statutory instruments. I think there are three steps in achieving the kind of parliamentary surveillance of statutory instruments which Professor Mallory argues to be necessary, which the Committee on Statutory Instruments deems to be necessary and which the bill before us indicates the government itself considers to be necessary. The first is publicity, making sure that the regulation has been promulgated and made known in order that people can examine it and see what its effects are likely to be. This is provided for in the bill
before us by the requirement that regulations be gazetted and otherwise publicized.
The second requirement is that there be some means of scrutinizing the regulations to make sure that they conform with clearly understood principles governing delegated legislation. Such mechanism is provided by clause 26 of the bill which deals with the establishment of a parliamentary committee. The third requirement, if there is to be adequate surveillance of delegated legislation, is that provision be made for some means of remedy when a regulation is considered to be unwise. Provision for this is made in the bill in the case of certain specific acts. I refer to clause 30 which does this, fundamentally, though it does so in a manner which gives Parliament less power than it has at present; it provides that a negative resolution of the House of Commons can result in a regulation being revoked. Nevertheless, there is no general provision for remedy in the bill.
Having outlined these three requirements, I think it becomes readily apparent that the type of committee to be established under clause 26 to scrutinize subordinate legislation, and its terms of reference, will have great influence upon the effectiveness of the measure before us. In my opinion the definiton of the role of the committee, as referred to in the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), is of great importance. The essential effect of that amendment lies in paragraph 3 in which the hon. member says:
Where a statutory instrument stands referred to such committee, the committee has, in respect to such statutory instrument, the power to recommend that the same be approved, varied or repealed.
Moreover, it is necessary to adopt some procedure which will ensure that Parliament can rapidly effect a remedy should the scrutiny committee feel it necessary to recommend that the regulation be varied, repealed or amended. Under the present rules of the House, what options are open to us? First there is the option of raising the matter under the terms of Standing Order 58(5). This order deals with the days allotted to the opposition, days on which the opposition may select a topic for debate. There is some difficulty about this approach because opposition parties must already choose from among a number of conflicting and urgent claims upon this allowance of time in the House.
Another option would be to resort to the use of Standing Order 26 when it came to the attention of the House through the scrutiny committee that a regulation needed to be amended or repealed. However, difficulty would be likely to arise here in connection with the question of urgency. I believe I can envisage circumstances in which a good many hon. members would deem it necessary for a regulation to be repealed but in which Mr. Speaker would be correct in ruling that the matter was not properly one for debate under the terms of Standing Order 26 because it was not sufficiently urgent or of general application.
Another option would be to take action under the terms of Standing Order 39A which allows an hon. member who has asked a question of a minister in the

March 10, 1971

House, and received what he considers to be an unsatisfactory reply, to raise the matter at the time of adjournment. In this case, though, only two people are allowed to engage in debate on the subject under discussion and I do not think this is sufficient guarantee that the House has available adequate means of remedy should it consider there is need to vary or repeat a regulation.
It is on this basis that I support the kind of provision suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in amendment No. 4. I refer to paragraph 3 of the amendment which reads as follows:
In the event that the said committee should in any report recommend the amendment, replacement or annulment of any statutory instrument, such report shall be brought on for consideration in the House of Commons within 15 sitting days after the tabling thereof in the same session, should such be possible, or within the first 20 sitting days in the next session following, and any debate thereon should continue subject to the Standing Orders of the House of Commons until the report shall have been finally disposed of.
I realize the minister has given the House an assurance that the terms of reference of the committee to be established under this legislation will meet the points raised by hon. members in their amendments and by those of us who speak in support of those amendments. However, since the committee to be established under clause 26 really represents the only means of scrutiny of delegated legislation, the only possible vehicle for redress, I am sure the minister will understand our reluctance to let the bill get out of our hands until we have received definite assurance from him that the problems we have drawn to his attention will be met in the terms of reference of the new committee. I am sure he will understand, too, that we would like to see these guarantees placed within the framework of the bill itself.
Speaking about the nature of the committee to be established by this legislation, there are two other factors I wish to bring to the minister's attention. The first is that the committee to be established must be adequately staffed. I suggest to the minister that he give serious consideration to basing that staff upon the legal counsel of Mr. Speaker and their staffs. It is not enough for such a committee to be assisted by members of the legal staff of the Department of Justice, because it is important that the committee, as a servant of this House and not of the government, should have the services of persons whose loyalties are completely undivided. In this regard I think it is an analagous situation to the relationship between the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee.
The other suggestion I wish to make in regard to the form of this committee is that it be empowered to deal not only with the form of statutory instruments or regulations but also with their substance. That is, it must deal with more than questions such as: Is the regulation clearly drafted? Is it based on statutory authority? Is it certain that it does not employ such wide and sweeping powers that constitutional principles are offended?
Such a committee should also be able to decide whether a regulation is a normal or an unusual and unexpected use of statutory authority. In this regard I would draw to
Statutory Instruments Act
the attention of the minister the suggestion of my colleague from Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) that one of the powers of the committee should be to refer the substance of a regulation to another and appropriate standing committee of the House.
In his remarks on Monday, I believe it was, the hon. member for Peace River drew the attention of the House to certain recommendations made by the Committee on Statutory Instruments dealing with the nature and function of the scrutiny committee to be established. He drew the attention of the House to the recommendation that the committee be allowed a preview of regulations so that before they come into force there might be an opportunity for Members of Parliament to express their opinions upon the validity of a regulation, its utility, its conformity to the statutory authority, and so forth.
In this regard I should like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that this particular power for the committee has not been included in the bill. Further, there will be certain regulations that are entirely excluded from the attention of the scrutiny committee. I find some difficulty in my approach to this question. What I really want to do is draw the problem to the minister's attention in the hope that he can clarify the issue for us in his remarks on these two amendments. I can deal with the matter very briefly.
Clause 27(c), on page 13 of the bill, empowers the Governor in Council to make regulations exempting any regulation or class of regulation from publication or scrutiny "in the interest of international relations, national defence or security, or federal-provincial relations". This is a pretty wide and sweeping power of exemption, and it bothers me. But what really concerns me is the seeming lack of provision in this bill similar to that in the Regulations Act requiring the exempting order itself to be published. This bill does provide for wider dissemination of information on statutory instruments, and therefore perhaps the wider powers of exemption are in order. But in their present form they are very wide indeed, with no assurance at all that anyone would get to know about the exemptions. I consider that to be a very dangerous feature of this bill, though perhaps I have misunderstood the situation. I would very much appreciate the minister devoting some attention to this problem when he eventually comments on these amendments, even though I am perhaps ranging a little far from the subject in drawing this matter to his attention.
Publication of an exempting order would at least alert a parliamentary committee or an opposition party to make discreet inquiries about why it was felt necessary to publish the exempting order. If that is not enough, then the committee or opposition party could raise the matter publicly. However, it seems to me that as this bill is presently constituted, parliamentary committees and Members of Parliament would not even know that a regulation had been exempted from the necessity for publication and, as I have said before, I consider this highly dangerous. I think the publication of an exempting order is a necessary safeguard. I should like to hear the minister's comments on the reason for the exclusion of
March 10, 1971

such a provision from this bill when he chooses to make his remarks on these two amendments.

speechtext:
That Bill C-182, an act to provide for the examination, publication and scrutiny of regulations and other statutory instruments, be amended by deleting therefrom clause 30 at page 18.
He said: Mr. Speaker, after some of the fireworks we have enjoyed during the last day and a half of debate in respect of what may seem a very mild resolution, I venture to suggest there is probably more dynamite in what I suggest in this motion than there is in the motions of my colleagues. I shall explain briefly what I regard as an extraordinarily important motion.
The effect of what is proposed here would be the knocking out of clause 30 on page 18 of the bill. This would mean that section 41 of the Defence Production Act of 1955 would be restored. Most parliamentarians are

perhaps not aware of the significance of section 41 of the Defence Production Act of 1955. I am certain that members of the press gallery are not aware of its significance, because there is only one pressman there at the moment. The fact is that the debate of 1955 was one of the two or three significant debates which has occurred in this chamber since the end of the Second World War. That alone should make one pause and consider what the minister and the government are attempting to do here.
Perhaps the situation is even more compounded and the confusion more confused by virtue of the fact that the bill most members have on their desk is Bill C-182 as it was originally returned from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. This is not the original bill presented to us on November 3, 1970. This is important, because unless hon. members have referred to the original bill, as well as members of the press gallery, they will not know what is taking place. In the bill presented to us for first reading there was an element of explanation. That explanation is not given in the reprinted bill. Let me turn to the page opposite page 18 of the original bill presented on November 3 and read from section 41 of the Defence Production Act, which would be repealed if we accept the bill now before us. I think this is important. It reads:
Every regulation, as defined in the Regulations Act, made under the authority of this act that is required to be laid before Parliament under section 7 of the Regulations Act and every regulation made under section 9 of the Regulations Act in relation to a regulation made under this act, shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament as soon as may be after it is made.
(2) Where a regulation has been laid before Parliament pursuant to subsection (1), a notice of motion in either House signed by ten members thereof, and made in accordance with the rules of that House within seven days of the day the regulation was laid before that House, praying that the regulation be revoked or amended, shall be debated in that House at the first convenient opportunity within the four sitting days next after the day the motion in that House was made.
I hope hon. members now start to prick up their ears and realize that something special was laid down in subsection 2. Perhaps we should ask ourselves why this provision was laid down in an act passed by a Liberal government in 1955. We should also ask ourselves what will happen in this regard as a result of the measure we are now considering. To complete the story I should read subsection 3 of this act passed by Parliament. It provides as follows:
A regulation that has been laid before Parliament pursuant to this section need not be laid before Parliament under section 7 or 9 of the Regulations Act, but nothing in this section shall be construed as affecting or limiting the obligation under section 6 of the Regulations Act to publish the regulation in the Canada Gazette.
Subsection 3 is not germane to the argument I am advancing, but this is the law of the land as it now stands. Section 41 (2) of the Defence Production Act provides that ten members of this place can sign a notice of motion to the effect that they do not like a regulation and ask that it be revoked or amended. That notice of motion has to be debated. The subsection does not say it may be debated, or that it may be put on some list, to be

drawn out of a hat and taken up in due course. It says it shall be debated. Section 41 (2) provides that the regulations shall be debated in the House at the first convenient opportunity within the four sitting days next after the day of the motion in the House. That is the law as it stands. In a moment I will explain some of the circumstances that led to the adoption of that provision. Let us compare that with what we find on page 18, clause 30 of the bill. It provides:
Section 41 of the Defence Production Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"41. Every regulation, as defined in the Statutory Instruments Act, made under the authority of this act is subject to negative resolution of Parliament.
Again I ask members to prick up their ears. I ask our faithful reporter in the press gallery to prick up his ears. Each of us must ask ourselves the question: What on earth is a negative resolution as suggested in this section of the act? The answer is that nobody in this chamber can remember such an animal as a negative resolution. Never has there been one proposed or considered in this chamber. There have been some proposed and debated in other parliaments. Perhaps we have a hint as to what a negative resolution is: it would seem to be something that destroys a resolution.
As a matter of procedure, one can search our rule book from cover to cover without finding any procedure, suggestion or practice in respect of a negative resolution in this House of Commons. We are in effect being asked to replace something which was fought out in this House of Commons in 1955 and adopted, even though the procedure has never been used. We are being asked to throw that away and replace it with something that is called "subject to negative resolution of Parliament", a procedure which we simply do not have in existence. This is a positive thing being cast away for something that may or may not provide for some parliamentary action one day. I think I have set the stage in respect of what we are being asked to do and perhaps for what I am suggesting we do not do. I give the minister the alternative. If we are to have a negative resolution procedure, it should be spelled out clearly in respect of application or commitment by the government. In that way we will know where we are going.
I turn now to the background of the reasons section 41 of the Defence Production Act was adopted. I shall do so by referring to a book which was placed in the hands of hon. members a short time ago. It was written by Alderman William Kilbourn and is entitled "Pipeline". At page 101 he characterizes the debate that took place in this chamber in 1955. I have already suggested that this was probably one of the two or three most important debates held in this House since the end of the Second World War. He sums it up in this way; and this will save going through several volumes of Hansard for the year 1955. I can compress what happened in that debate by reading one paragraph at the top of page 101. At the bottom of page 100 he is dealing with the start of the pipeline debate-but as we all know, that was the forerunner. It reads as follows:
Statutory Instruments Act
The opposition for the first time sensed the possibility of a major victory in the House of Commons. They had already succeeded in the summer of 1955 in forcing Howe's first public defeat by splitting the cabinet on the issue of the indefinite extension of his powers in the Defence Production Act. Since Howe's powers as Minister of Defence Production could make him "the virtual dictator of the whole economy," as Donald Fleming put it, they dug in and fought for a compromise. Some members of the cabinet who half agreed with such criticism were a good deal more anxious than Howe to avoid a summer-long filibuster. While Howe was prepared for some concessions, he rejected the idea of any time limit on his emergency powers. During his absence over a long weekend he left the matter with his colleagues to act as they saw fit. Prime Minister St. Laurent and opposition leader Drew arrived at a compromise which in effect was a capitulation to Drew's terms. As one observer put it, it was "the issue on which George Drew enjoyed his greatest hour of triumph in the House". The Liberals had barely concealed division in their own ranks and then retreated despite their vastly superior numbers. Howe was furious when he heard the news, and summoned House leader Walter Harris to his House of Commons office. St. Laurent got wind of this and within moments of Harris's arrival, slipped into Howe's office unannounced, and nodded to Harris to leave. St. Laurent told Howe that the decision to compromise was entirely his own, and there the matter ended.
When Alderman Kilbourn says that the matter ended, what really happened was that in the House of Commons the Defence Production Act was amended with that compromise, so that the right that was won by the opposition in those days in a bitter debate was secured by the passage of section 41 of the act, the section that we are now being asked to repeal. So it is perhaps not surprising that when this issue came before the justice committee I had the following to say, as recorded in issue No. 7 of the proceedings of Tuesday, February 16, of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs:
This caused quite considerable debate back in 1955 when it was brought in and just offhand perhaps Mr. Beseau-

-could answer my question because it seems to me we may have watered down the right here. Under the procedure established in that year you could get notice signed by ten members. I wonder whether we could have a comment on that.

As long as I have such august gentlemen talking about this problem I will be very happy, because to me at least it is a pretty substantial one and I hope that I can enlist from the back benches whatever weight hon. members can bring to bear on this problem. As I said, we are left with the option of replacing a very definite procedure, albeit one that has not been used to my knowledge, with a procedure that has not been accepted by the House and would be set forth in the statute. It may be years before the House gets around to dealing with its procedure in this direction.
I do not know about the effect of the suggestion on the rules of the other place, but by that statute there is a clear direction to go through the statutory process of enactment, namely, first reading, second reading, committee of the whole and third reading. We now have a slightly different procedure, but legislation still goes through first reading, second reading and consideration in committee. Then it comes back to the House, through report stage if there is any question about it, and then third reading. Compare that with the process of setting up rules and regulations by the House where you have referral to a committee. The committee may struggle for a long time or a short time with it. Then it comes back to the House and the committee's report is presumably adopted or varied in some way.
There are several complications in establishing a procedure by way of statute, more so than by establishing it through the rules of the House. Because it is more complicated, I suggest it gives a greater right. It is difficult to disentangle something like section 41 of the Defence Production Act and that is why I am fighting for it and making the best argument I can. It may be said that the repeal of this section is of little moment because it deals with procedure, but some of us can recall great words of wisdom from a former justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, Mr. Justice Rand. These words have always appealed to me because he was a Maritimer. He was asked about the development of jurisprudence in so far as it affected human rights and fundamental freedoms in Canada, and he said, "The procedure is the source and protection of all our rights." In short, a right is meaningless and non-existent unless we can invoke it. If we feel that our rights are infringed upon, we can scream in one direction, write a notice in another direction or summon up some procedure whereby our complaint will be looked at.

March 10, 1971

I would also point out that a pretty substantial right was won by a minority in Parliament. For example, it was a right that our friends to my far left, with the support of only one or two other members, could have used if they felt that the regulations under the Defence Production Act were in any way wrong. It was a right that members solely within the ranks of the NDP could use, or any group within the official opposition or, for that matter, within the rump that sits alongside Your Honour, or on the other side flanked around the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his group. As I say, it was a pretty substantial right and probably was as good a check as one could have found on the powers of a minister who had grown so used to power that probably he was a little indifferent to the processes by which power is granted to a minister. That is my argument and I will not belabour it. I think I have put all my points on the record.
I understand that negotiations have been going on all around me even while I am still on my feet, Mr. Speaker. I am just trying to catch the flavour of them and also to present my concluding peroration. Since my contribution seems to have had some effect, I will conclude by saying I hope I get from the Minister of Justice an amplification of the assurance that he provided in committee, namely, that we would learn a little more about this mystic right known as the negative resolution. Then if we have to march off in new directions in the law, we will carry with us the spirit of something that was fought for and won in 1955 in this Chamber.

The amendment must be carefully read. Clause 28A(l)(a) reads:
In every act, (a) the expression "subject to affirmative resolution of Parliament", when used in relation to any regulation means that-
The only point is that none of the statutes that lie behind us have the phrase "subject to affirmative resolution of Parliament" or "subject to negative resolution of Parliament". under the act should stand still until they have been either approved or negatived by Parliament.

-or if Parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first seven days next thereafter that Parliament is sitting, praying that the regulation be revoked or amended, shall be debated in that House at the first convenient opportunity within the four sitting days next after the day the motion in that House was made.

That is all that is contained in the Defence Production Act amendment-and this is a parallel argument. If the minister was prepared to accept the argument in that case, why not in the others?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR EXAMINATION, PUBLICATION AND SCRUTINY
speechtext:
If there were more open minds and fewer open mouths we might get somewhere. Let me refer to the bill itself. This debate has been fascinating because it has indicated that in reality it is the civil servants who run the affairs of this country. Our affairs are conducted by bureaucratically-oriented civil servants with the assistance of aspirants to the cabinet on the other side of the House. I must make certain exceptions in respect of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), who raised his eyes when I made that remark, and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene). I am sure he is able to establish his credentials but he has not presented them up to now. It is the civil servants, with the aid of volcanic exchanges between the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and others, with belches of smoke and lava, who run the country. These are the people who deal with the affairs of this country by means of statutory instruments and regulations.
To illustrate the position let me point out that out of 600 statutes on our books, 430 have been created by Order in Council, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by tribunals or by other innocuous bodies. If we were to consider the last ten years on a percentage basis, I am convinced that a much higher percentage of our statutes has been created or amended than the 70 per cent I have referred to in respect of the figure of 430 out of 600.
The other day during a debate in the House of Commons the Minister of Justice participated in some interesting exchanges. In particular, I had occasion to refer the minister to recommendations of the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments, whose report was the basis upon which the minister brought in this measure. Some of us in the House worked a long time on this matter. I give credit to members who sit on the government side as well as those of other parties. We created what we feel is a good example of legislation in respect of statutory instruments and regulations. We obtained a consensus of hon. members in respect of changes that should be made. These are changes which the government has avoided.
I suggest that the government's bill falls far short of the proposals put forward by the special committee. The Minister of Justice took issue with me in this regard by referring to the recommendations contained in the Mac-Guigan report. In this regard I intend to meet him in the same way because I think this is an important matter. Among the proposals of the committee was one in respect of a change in dealing with statutory enactments. Many suggestions were made by the committee which could and should form policy of the government in this particularly vexatious and difficult situation. In addition, there were proposals in respect of the establishment of a committee of scrutiny. In this regard the committee made a categorical recommendation.

March 10, 1971
Statutory Instruments Act
The Minister of Justice said he could not meet us in this regard and that the House itseli should be the instrument through which the committee was established. He suggested this House should set up the terms of reference. I agree with him basically in most respects. Having in mind the stage to which we have advanced, I think it would be wrong for us to pass this bill without first obtaining from the Minister of Justice, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and the Prime Minister-I am convinced they are now discussing this matter with an eye to agreeing with me-an assurance that a large percentage of the proposals made by the special committee will be adopted.
The Minister of Justice has indicated that it is his intention to bring about the establishment of a special committee with powers parallel or equivalent to those the committee proposed. He has given us the assurance, as a member of the government, that this will be done. This is still a matter for cabinet decision before a resolution is presented. We may wait until the end of this session or perhaps the next session before witnessing any attempt by the government to create such a committee. Without the establishment of such a committee and the passage of this bill, Parliament will be useless.
I suggest there should be a categorical statement on behalf of the government that there will be introduced to this House within a specified period of time legislation setting up the appropriate committee. This could be achieved as the result of discussion among the Government House Leader and leaders of the other parties. By agreement they could decide the terms of reference. Anything short of that falls far short of achievement of any value.
Let us examine the recommendations found at pages 90, 91, 92 and 93 of this report. The report contains a very cogent series of proposals which the Minister of Justice has not seen fit to introduce; he has made an attempt to slough them of. Proposal No. 2 is:
Except in the interests of national security, there should be no exemptions from the requirements of the Regulations Act other than as to publication.
The bill goes much further than that in its restrictive effect. As I understand it, an amendment will be introduced later and I do not intend to go too far into this matter. I do not intend to say anything about what has been accomplished, because this bill goes far beyond the restrictive effects proposed in the recommendation. The recommendations continue:
The Minister of Justice should be charged with the responsibility of deciding for all regulation-making authorities which documents should be classified as regulations.
That is not the case. A committee of civil servants has been established and there have been terms agreed upon which direct that there shall be liaison among the Minister of Justice, the deputy minister, the department and the committee. What we now have in so far as this bill is concerned is one committee of civil servants sitting in judgment, deciding on the character of restrictions which should exist in respect of regulations and Orders in Council. What we have in mind is a committee answerable through the Minister of Justice, who is an elected representative of the people, through the medium of questions in the House of Commons, to Members of Parliament. We must be in a position to make sure he is discharging his responsibility as minister, particularly in the establishment of this committee.
The minister has suggested that the recommendation in this regard has been met. We believe such a provision is very important. I am sure that hon. members on this side, as well as those who sit opposite, will agree with me and the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Gibson) that it was made crystal clear that the committee felt the Minister of Justice was ultimately responsible. The minister could delegate that responsibility but we would be entitled to look to him for answers to our questions. However, the bill does make this provision.
We went on to recommend that all enabling acts in respect of regulation-making authorities should meet certain principles. I agree that when we come to examine those it is very difficult to include in statute form the kind of restrictions and proposals which were made by the committee. But I think we should have such a declaration by this government, which I admit is not binding on future governments; and there will be another government within a comparatively short time-as to that there is no doubt. While not binding on other governments, there should be a declaration by this government as a matter of principle, either a written declaration or a statement in the House on motions, that with respect to the enactment, promulgation and the type of regulations which will be passed, basically the proposals contained in recommendation 7 will be followed.
In saying this I concede that the minister would have a problem in putting all the recommendations into statutory form. I will not read them all; they are available to all Members of Parliament. But it is my submission that the failure to do this constitutes a grave breach of what the committee had in mind when it laid down this series of recommendations in its report.
Under recommendation 8 the Minister of Justice should refer the enabling clauses to the proposed standing committee on regulations at the same time as the bill is referred. That cannot be put in statutory form either, but I think it is a useful suggestion and I throw it out so it may be followed. What happens when we are discussing in this House on second reading bills which contain a regulatory-granting power? We will always find in those bills one clause which enables the Governor in Council to deal with regulations. I would think that if there is serious doubt in the minds of the government or of the minister involved, the matter should be referred to a committee with special reference to examine the issue before the statute is passed, or contemporaneously while it is being considered. All too often we find that the simple, sometimes insidious words contained in these regulatory-granting powers and in the regulations go far beyond what was contemplated and have effects which were not in the minds of the members who were dealing with the issue.

March 10, 1971

I read recommendation 9 when I was speaking on my motion. I do not think it would do any harm to summarize it. Before making regulations, regulation-making authorities should engage in the widest possible consultation with the public at large as well as with those most directly affected. I think that is probably one of the most important functions to be considered. When regulations are enacted they do not have the publicity which statutes receive when they are being discussed in the House. I am not suggesting it should apply to every regulation but when we are dealing with questions of transportation, for example, it should apply. Another typical example is immigration regulations. There is no doubt that there are in existence a number of regulations which are not within the knowledge of a great many people in this country. I would say that 99 per cent of the members of this House do not know what these regulations are. They do not know whom they affect and what could be their result.
I think it would be wise in situations where important matters are being considered that advance notice be given and that there be an opportunity for representations to be made by members of the public as to what the regulations should be. We hear all this mockery about participatory democracy, but I think without some opportunity being given for the public to be advised, to be warned, to make its comments as to what regulations are going to be enacted, regulations which more than statutes affect us seriously, we are not dealing adequately with the subject.
There are many other recommendations which I will not take the time of the House to read. I want to conclude on this note. I repeat what I said before. I urge, first, that a statement be made on behalf of the government indicating that there will be brought into the House within a reasonable time before this session is ended, proposed amendments to the Standing Orders which will provide for the establishment of a committee of scrutiny and the terms of reference of that committee. Second, there should be made, on behalf of the government, by a responsible minister a statement that in dealing with regulations the recommendations made by the special committee will follow as closely as possible. These are the kind of recommendations which cannot come into a statute but which form the pith and substance, the essence of our proposals to this House. Without those statements being made I say that this House is being short-changed by this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very briefly I would like to add to the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) that I am very sorry that I do not have the enthusiasm for this bill that I had hoped to have. I feel, as I indicated to the minister, that this bill was designed by the Department of Justice for the benefit of the officials of that department. It creates a fine administrative sieve. In my view, statutory instruments may have to go through such an administrative sieve; but the purpose of the whole exercise, right from the time proposals were made in the House for setting up this committee, and the
Statutory Instruments Act
burden of all the argument has been that there shall be a review by Parliament, because statutory instruments are delegated legislation and surely to goodness Parliament has the right to review.
A partial step only has been taken. The legislation says that there will be a scrutiny committee, and that is all. The exceptions to the regulations that will be referred to this scrutiny committee are fairly wide; As a matter of fact, they are too wide for my liking because unless they are published they do not go to the scrutiny committee. Particularly those that apply to a few people-and there are some exceptions to that in clause 11-go too far for real safety because there can be as great an injustice in a statutory instrument that applies to a limited class of people, or even to an individual, as there can be to one of general application; yet the limited ones are exempt from examination.
The third point I would like to make is that I regret that the minister has not seen fit to include in the legislation amendments to section 26. I will come back to the arguments I made. This is a grand gesture. There is authority now in the statute for Parliament to set up a scrutiny committee; but you have not given it any tools to work with-merely that certain classes of instruments shall stand referred to the committee and from there on there is nothing. This House has not one guarantee, one indication of any kind, saving and excepting, shall we say, the benevolent good wishes of the Minister of Justice that he will use his good offices with his colleagues, and so forth and so on, so that parliament might get a good resolution. But that is not enough.
We do not know, as my colleague from Peace River said, when this resolution is to come forward. Can the Minister of Justice in all honesty tell the House when we might expect such a resolution to come forward? Will it be this session or next session? The next question is: What will it contain?

There is no indication that the government will at any time bring in the changes. The resolution is entirely at the initiative of the government. There is not one opportunity for a backbencher or a private member from either side of the House to bring forward a resolution which would have the effect of getting this scrutiny committee established, or of setting down the procedures to be followed. And certainly to me this is a disappointment.
If the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth would only look at the logic of the amendment introduced this afternoon by the Minister of Justice with regard to section 41 of the Defence Production Act, he would see that what was included in it was precisely the same logic and the same general procedure that applied to the amendment to clause 26 that I put forward. However, under the Defence Production Act one does not move under the rules of Parliament. It states that on a motion signed by ten members the regulation should be brought on for debate within four sitting days after the motion is tabled.
My amendment provided for the report of a committee in which there was a recommendation for the variation, the annulment or the amendment of any statutory instrument, and that that report would be brought forward, debated and disposed of in government time. What is the difference between the two? They apply the same logic. It is not a question of rules determining how this is going to happen, but the statute lays it down. What is the difference? We should still have the resolution in the House to set up the scrutiny committee, but on this there was no undertaking.
I have been critical in certain respects but I know the minister will admit there there were a lot of areas in which there was agreement. I think the bill is a step forward, but I had hoped it could be that great bold step forward which the minister had hoped would come about. I regret that the minister was not quite as bold as he should have been. That is the burden of my criticism. We will keep after the minister to see that we get this scrutiny committee, not next year or the year after that: we want the appropriate resolution on the Order Paper in good time, with the knowledge that the House leaders are meeting to discuss its general terminology. I will leave the matter on that basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke earlier this afternoon I indicated that I was somewhat uneasy about one of the provisions in the bill empowering the Governor in Council to make regulations exempting regulations or classes of regulations from publication or scrutiny, in the interests of international relations, national defence, security or federal-provincial relations. That is a pretty sweeping set of powers given to the Governor in Council, powers which could cover a multitude of sins. As I indicated earlier this afternoon, perhaps wider powers of exemption than is the case under the Regulations Act are required because there are stronger provisions for publication in the bill now before us. But even so I am concerned that there is no explicit provision in this bill for the publication of the exemption order which would be made under the authority of clause 27 in any one of these four rather broad and all-encompassing areas.
I repeat that there is no specific provision in the bill that the regulation which exempts other regulations from publication or scrutiny must be published so that Members of Parliament and the public can be aware that such an exemption has taken place and, if they are interested in determining why such an exemption has been allowed, they can then make inquiries in order to determine the reasons for it. If they find the reasons unsatisfactory, they could bring the matter to the attention of the public and raise it publicly in this House. There is no specific provision for that in the bill. I consider this to be a rather glaring omission in the legislation. I think it is a lack of a proper safeguard which must be in the bill if it is to be the sort of legislation we want to see passed by this House.
I am very reluctant to do what I am about to do, because the minister has shown a considerable degree of co-operation with the House this afternoon in making accommodations to suggestions put forward by the opposition. In fact, I feel somewhat culpable in not having put forward this amendment at report stage where it properly fitted, but it is not something that came to my attention in time for me to do that. I think it is an indication of how serious an omission I think it is that I feel compelled to move the amendment which I am going to move at this time, even though it will somewhat delay the activities of the House. Nevertheless, I consider the omission of the right of the public to know a regulation has been exempted from the provisions for publication or scrutiny under the terms of the bill is something which we cannot allow to pass unchallenged. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill C-182 be not now read a third time but that it he referred back to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for the purpose of reconsidering clause 27 thereof.

Mr. Speaker, I can make my remarks in about two minutes. I regret that I did not bring in an amendment on second reading to deal with clause 27. I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) will recall that I did bring an amendment before the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee. I, too, feel that clause 27 provides for exemptions from the very salutary provisions of the bill, for publication and inspection of statutory instruments. I feel that it provides a dangerously wide breach which threatens to deprive the act of the effect which I think it should have and which I think Parliament would intend it to have.

March 10, 1971	COMMONS
I want to refer particularly to the provisions in clause 27 that allow exemption from the necessity of publication in the Canada Gazette of any statutory instrument which in the opinion of the Governor in Council would not be in the interests of federal-provincial relations. It seems to me that this is a very broad provision. In all democratic countries governments have used powers like this to exempt from publication and to seek to get behind some sort of curtain of secrecy, certain things that are done. If they are invited to do so by legislation, merely by a declaration that federal-provincial relations might be affected, we know how often that would prevent an instrument that ought to be published from coming to public attention. I regret doing it at this stage and I confess it is my oversight. I did not bring in an amendment at the report stage, but the matter is so important that I thought it should be brought forward now.

Mr. Speaker, I know that under the rules of the House I do not close debate at third reading stage, but it might be appropriate for me to say a few words because I feel the debate will close out and perhaps the vote could be agreed upon tomorrow. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) was all for having me give a number of undertakings. What I am saying now represents my attitude to the bill, and I think it is shared by the House leader. These matters have not been considered by executive council but I can say to him, first of all, that a resolution amending the Standing Orders with the effect of establishing a scrutiny committee will be presented at this session of Parliament to implement not only the recommendations of the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments but also to fulfil the provision of clause 26 of the bill before the House.
The hon. member for Peace River wanted me to give some sort of undertaking on the recommendations of the special committee's report. I can say to him that within the reservations I stated the other night when I analyzed the recommendations one by one, I favour, as does the government generally, the recommendations contained in the report. I intend to draw up some criteria implementing regulation No. 7, that is to say, those proposals that should govern enabling acts for regulation-making authority.
Hopefully, those criteria will be accepted by the government and will govern the drafting procedure of future statutes. I am hopeful that this will be done, but the ultimate control will be Parliament when statutes are brought forward. I would expect this House and the standing committee considering bills to compare the enabling statutes with the criteria in recommendation No. 7 of the report of the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments. Although the hon. member for Peace River did not mention it specifically, regulation 19 (9) of the report establishes criteria for the examination of regulations by the scrutiny committee. That being the case, I intend to have those criteria set forth in an internal cabinet directive before regulations are made and drafted in order to anticipate the criteria which the scrutiny committee would want to apply to those regulations.

In the enabling powers of bills themselves and as affecting the regulations that will be drafted and inspected by the Privy Council and the Deputy Minister of Justice, those criteria I hope will be binding internally and I will advance them within the framework of the recommendations. Hon. members can weigh what I am saying by referring to the statement that the then President of the Privy Council, now the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), made when he appeared on behalf of the government before the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments. That statement can be found in the evidence of the committee.
I hope that will deal satisfactorily with the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who was re-establishing the argument that he made in presenting his amendment at the report stage. I have nothing further to add except to say that he, and to a certain extent the hon. member for Peace River, feel that the scrutiny committee ought to be under an umbrella set forth in the statute itself. I believe the scrutiny committee ought to be governed by the Standing Orders of the House. But that is a matter for this House or the other place if it is a joint committee. That is basically the difference in our views.
Dealing now with the amendment of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland), supported by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), it is true that the hon. member for Greenwood did present an amendment to the standing committee. I dealt with the argument as to why those exemptions were what they were, and what the government's philosophy was in widening the exemptions beyond those established in the report. It is true that the special committee said the exemptions should merely be limited to national security, but we widened them and the reasons are found in the evidence given to the standing committee.
The hon. member for Selkirk made a valid point, that the problem of exemptions as such is that the scrutiny committee might not know what regulations have been exempted because there will be no record. All regulations for statutory instruments will go to the scrutiny committee, except those regulations that have been exempted from inspection by the public. They are limited to the criteria for international relations, federal-provincial relations, security and where they affect individual rights or involve specific classes of people or individuals found within clause 27 of the bill.
The regulations providing for the class of regulations that are to be exempt will be sent to the scrutiny committee. That committee will have before it the criteria as to the type of regulations which in future will be exempt. I think it is a matter for the scrutiny committee, the government and individual departments to work out from time to time. The hon. member has a valid point. There is no way of curing that when you get to matters which relate to security, and so on. We went through that intellectual exercise internally and did not come up with a satisfactory solution. But the committee will have the regulations under which exemptions are made.

In conclusion, I thank the House and hon. members for this constructive debate in which the highlights of the bill have been tested. Although privately hon. members, I think, concede that this is a step forward, I think that the bill will provide, in terms more optimistic than some hon. members are willing to concede, for a more open society for Canadians through their representatives in the House of Commons.
